title: Downlink TDoA - finally, the Indoor GPS we’ve been waiting for
summary: Your phone can guide you across a city. But step inside an airport, a hospital, or a shopping mall, and it can lose its way. GPS signals from satellites in the sky don’t work reliably indoors. We’ve been working on that problem at Estimote for more than a decade. Bluetooth beacons were our first-generation solution. They helped mobile developers experiment with new indoor experiences and imagine what location-aware apps could be. With iOS 27 publicly available today, Apple is opening another important door for developers. Its Nearby Interaction API now supports UWB Downlink TDoA without the special entitlement previously required. That puts a new generation of indoor location experiences within reach of iOS developers. We believe this is huge! A true Indoor GPS moment. Here’s why: We’ve been building toward this since iBeacon In 2013, when we launched our first product, we put small iBeacon-compatible beacons into developers’ hands. Suddenly, an app could react when someone entered a store, approached an exhibit, or arrived at a particular place. Physical proximity became something you could build software around. That first generation of indoor location opened up an entirely new set of ideas. It also showed us how much developers wanted reliable and scalable positioning inside buildings for their use cases. With Bluetooth proximity based on signal strength (RSSI), accuracy was only a few meters, and position estimates could fluctuate or jump around. The new UWB chip that Apple introduced in iPhones in 2019 brought superior positioning precision. However, one-to-one, two-way ranging made it difficult to scale, since only a limited number of users could use the same beacons for indoor positioning at the same time. In 2023, when Apple released its second-generation UWB chip, we wrote about Downlink TDoA as one of the most exciting possibilities. And it is finally true! Small anchors become indoor satellites DL-TDoA stands for Downlink Time Difference of Arrival. The name sounds more complicated than the idea. Small UWB transmitters, called anchors, are installed at known positions on walls or ceilings. They coordinate their timing and broadcast messages that let a receiving device, such as a phone, relate precise timing measurements to those positions. Your phone listens. It compares the differences in when signals arrive from multiple anchors and uses that information to calculate where it is with inch-level precision. Think of the anchors as a local constellation of indoor satellites or lighthouses. The analogy is about how positioning works: infrastructure broadcasts, and your device works out its own location. An equipped building still needs installed anchors, and your phone needs a UWB chip, a compatible app, and user permissions. Below, you can see a recording of position and heading estimates computed on an iPhone with iOS 27 in a 5 × 4 meter room with four UWB anchors compatible with DL-TDoA. Our typical deployments deliver around 20–30 cm positioning accuracy, depending on anchor placement, geometry, visibility, and post-processing. That opens up experiences at the scale of a doorway, a shelf, or a particular place within a room. A smart building guides you, but doesn’t track you One of the most interesting things about Downlink TDoA is where the calculation happens. The phone determines its position directly on the device. The UWB positioning calculation does not require the phone to connect or to send its location back to the anchors. That is very privacy-friendly and doesn’t allow users to be tracked without their explicit permission. Another benefit of this passive listen-and-compute architecture is scalability. There is no limit to how many phones can use anchors to compute their positions. This architecture is a perfect fit for large and busy public spaces, such as airport terminals filling with passengers, underground stations, or stadiums welcoming thousands of fans. App developers can design mobile apps that enable users to share their location for various services. Users remain in control: they can disable location sharing or delete the app, just as with GPS positioning. The standard is what makes this bigger We’ve seen various indoor location technologies over the years. What makes DL-TDoA exciting is the combination of precise UWB positioning, an architecture that broadcasts to many devices at once, industry standardization, and support from major phone manufacturers such as Apple and Google. The FiRa Consortium, an organization that standardizes UWB and whose members include Apple and Google, has spent years developing UWB specifications and certification programs to make devices interoperable. Downlink TDoA is part of that work. The interoperability of this standard extends the opportunity not only to compatible phones, but also to robots, drones, smart glasses, and other devices, all using the same indoor positioning infrastructure to compute their precise positions. For us, this is the long-awaited shift to a new generation of indoor location. Developers can build around shared indoor positioning infrastructure and spend more of their time creating the experiences people have been imagining for years. New APIs in iOS 27 Apple introduced UWB chips to the iPhone in 2019. Their first use case was Precision Finding for AirTag. In 2020, Apple opened up UWB access through the Nearby Interaction API. With iOS 27, that API has been extended to support DL-TDoA. In the API, you’ll find the NIDLTDOAConfiguration method. This tells the phone how it will receive the UWB configuration of a nearby DL-TDoA cluster when you walk into range. The phone can receive it silently over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. Once the phone knows the exact UWB configuration, you’ll see a stream of NIDLTDOAMeasurement updates. These are timing measurements from nearby anchors that you can use to compute an indoor position. You can do this yourself, or you can use our iOS SDK, which computes the position for you and returns a stream of X and Y coordinates. We have an entire system called SpaceTimeOS that makes it easy to deploy DL-TDoA anchor clusters at scale and use them with mobile SDKs. What can you build with it? Imagine an airport app that continues guiding you after you step inside the terminal, all the way to the right gate or even to your seat inside the aircraft. Or a retail app that guides you to the shelf holding the product you searched for. A new workplace app could show the relevant instructions when you enter a particular environment or approach a machine or piece of equipment. See more use-cases on our website. How to get started with Downlink TDoA? We’ve got you covered! We’ve been working for quite some time to develop compatible hardware, firmware, and SDKs that help developers quickly dive into this new technology. To get started with DL-TDoA, all you need are our UWB Anchors. We have a Dev Kit with four anchors that you can set up in your room to create the first cluster. We’ve spent years helping developers make their apps location- and context-aware. Downlink TDoA brings us closer to the experience we’ve wanted all along: precise indoor positioning, built on an interoperable standard, with location calculated in a privacy-friendly way directly on the phone. We can’t wait to see what you build!
body_markdown:
Your phone can guide you across a city. But step inside an airport, a hospital, or a shopping mall, and it can lose its way. GPS signals from satellites in the sky don’t work reliably indoors.


We’ve been working on that problem at Estimote for more than a decade. Bluetooth beacons were our first-generation solution. They helped mobile developers experiment with new indoor experiences and imagine what location-aware apps could be.


With iOS 27 publicly available today, Apple is opening another important door for developers. Its Nearby Interaction API now supports UWB Downlink TDoA without the special entitlement previously required. That puts a new generation of indoor location experiences within reach of iOS developers.


We believe this is huge! A true Indoor GPS moment. Here’s why:


W **e’ve been building toward this since iBeacon**
In 2013, when we launched our first product, we put small iBeacon-compatible beacons into developers’ hands. Suddenly, an app could react when someone entered a store, approached an exhibit, or arrived at a particular place. Physical proximity became something you could build software around.


That first generation of indoor location opened up an entirely new set of ideas. It also showed us how much developers wanted reliable and scalable positioning inside buildings for their use cases.


With Bluetooth proximity based on signal strength (RSSI), accuracy was only a few meters, and position estimates could fluctuate or jump around.


The new UWB chip that Apple introduced in iPhones in 2019 brought superior positioning precision. However, one-to-one, two-way ranging made it difficult to scale, since only a limited number of users could use the same beacons for indoor positioning at the same time.


In 2023, when Apple released its second-generation UWB chip,[we wrote about Downlink TDoA](https://blog.estimote.com/post/728317898359259136/whats-exciting-about-u2-the-second-gen-uwb-chip) as one of the most exciting possibilities. And it is finally true!


**Small anchors become indoor satellites**


DL-TDoA stands for Downlink Time Difference of Arrival. The name sounds more complicated than the idea.


Small UWB transmitters, called anchors, are installed at known positions on walls or ceilings. They coordinate their timing and broadcast messages that let a receiving device, such as a phone, relate precise timing measurements to those positions.


Your phone listens. It compares the differences in when signals arrive from multiple anchors and uses that information to calculate where it is with inch-level precision.


Think of the anchors as a local constellation of indoor satellites or lighthouses. The analogy is about how positioning works: infrastructure broadcasts, and your device works out its own location. An equipped building still needs installed anchors, and your phone needs a UWB chip, a compatible app, and user permissions.


Below, you can see a recording of position and heading estimates computed on an iPhone with iOS 27 in a 5 × 4 meter room with four UWB anchors compatible with DL-TDoA.


Our typical deployments deliver around 20–30 cm positioning accuracy, depending on anchor placement, geometry, visibility, and post-processing. That opens up experiences at the scale of a doorway, a shelf, or a particular place within a room.


**A smart building guides you, but doesn’t track you**


One of the most interesting things about Downlink TDoA is where the calculation happens.


The phone determines its position directly on the device. The UWB positioning calculation does not require the phone to connect or to send its location back to the anchors. That is very privacy-friendly and doesn’t allow users to be tracked without their explicit permission.


Another benefit of this passive listen-and-compute architecture is scalability. There is no limit to how many phones can use anchors to compute their positions. This architecture is a perfect fit for large and busy public spaces, such as airport terminals filling with passengers, underground stations, or stadiums welcoming thousands of fans.


App developers can design mobile apps that enable users to share their location for various services. Users remain in control: they can disable location sharing or delete the app, just as with GPS positioning.


**The standard is what makes this bigger**


We’ve seen various indoor location technologies over the years. What makes DL-TDoA exciting is the combination of precise UWB positioning, an architecture that broadcasts to many devices at once, industry standardization, and support from major phone manufacturers such as Apple and Google.


The FiRa Consortium, an organization that standardizes UWB and whose members include Apple and Google, has spent years developing UWB specifications and certification programs to make devices interoperable. Downlink TDoA is part of that work. The interoperability of this standard extends the opportunity not only to compatible phones, but also to robots, drones, smart glasses, and other devices, all using the same indoor positioning infrastructure to compute their precise positions.


For us, this is the long-awaited shift to a new generation of indoor location. Developers can build around shared indoor positioning infrastructure and spend more of their time creating the experiences people have been imagining for years.


**New APIs in iOS 27**


Apple introduced UWB chips to the iPhone in 2019. Their first use case was Precision Finding for AirTag. In 2020, Apple opened up UWB access through the Nearby Interaction API. With iOS 27, that API has been extended to support DL-TDoA.


In the API, you’ll find the NIDLTDOAConfiguration method. This tells the phone how it will receive the UWB configuration of a nearby DL-TDoA cluster when you walk into range. The phone can receive it silently over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth.


Once the phone knows the exact UWB configuration, you’ll see a stream of NIDLTDOAMeasurement updates. These are timing measurements from nearby anchors that you can use to compute an indoor position.


You can do this yourself, or you can use our iOS SDK, which computes the position for you and returns a stream of X and Y coordinates. We have an entire system called SpaceTimeOS that makes it easy to deploy DL-TDoA anchor clusters at scale and use them with mobile SDKs.


**What can you build with it?**


Imagine an airport app that continues guiding you after you step inside the terminal, all the way to the right gate or even to your seat inside the aircraft. Or a retail app that guides you to the shelf holding the product you searched for. A new workplace app could show the relevant instructions when you enter a particular environment or approach a machine or piece of equipment. See[more use-cases on our website](https://estimote.com/index.html#use-cases) .


**How to get started with Downlink TDoA?**


We’ve got you covered! We’ve been working for quite some time to develop compatible hardware, firmware, and SDKs that help developers quickly dive into this new technology.


To get started with DL-TDoA, all you need are our[UWB Anchors.](https://estimote.com/dl-tdoa) We have a Dev Kit with four anchors that you can set up in your room to create the first cluster.


We’ve spent years helping developers make their apps location- and context-aware. Downlink TDoA brings us closer to the experience we’ve wanted all along: precise indoor positioning, built on an interoperable standard, with location calculated in a privacy-friendly way directly on the phone.


We can’t wait to see what you build!
